title: PVGas bad debt, Q1/2026
subtitle: Receivables, concentration risk and the quality of revenue
openingQuestion: What do bad debts and large receivables usually affect first?
explanation: Large receivables and high customer concentration can make revenue look attractive while cash flow deteriorates and credit risk rises. If a handful of large customers account for most of the revenue and they run into financial trouble, the business may have to book a large and unexpected bad-debt provision.

realWorldExample.description: A gas business sells most of its output to a small group of industrial customers - mainly power and fertiliser plants. The structure has real advantages: long-term contracts, forecastable volume, low selling costs. The downside shows up when one customer pays late: for a retail chain, losing a customer costs a thousandth of revenue; here one customer can be a double-digit percentage. So reading a business like this means looking at two things the headline statements do not show: the largest customer's share of revenue, and the ageing of receivables. Revenue rising steadily while the ageing lengthens is a sign that cash is stuck, not that trading is good.

quiz.question: What does receivables growing faster than revenue suggest?
options: The business is certainly getting healthier
The two figures have nothing to do with each other
The business is collecting its cash more slowly
This year's dividend will be higher than last year's
quiz.explanation: When receivables jump, accounting profit can look better than the actual cash flow. Sales are being recognised while the money sits with the customer. The two figures are tightly linked, since receivables are simply the revenue that has not been collected yet; and nothing about a slower collection cycle points to a bigger dividend - if anything the cash to pay one is exactly what is missing.

quiz.question: A company earns 70% of its revenue from 3 large customers. How does this concentration risk affect the valuation of the business?
options: No effect, since revenue has been stable year after year
Always valued higher, because large customers are more reliable
Only an accounting matter, with no bearing on the valuation
Value it more conservatively - losing one customer costs a lot
quiz.explanation: Concentration risk is a genuine business risk: losing one large customer can cause an immediate revenue loss the business cannot easily replace, quite unlike losing one of thousands of small customers. Investors normally demand a larger margin of safety, or pay a lower multiple, for businesses with high concentration risk. Past stability says nothing about the risk, and size makes a customer's failure more damaging rather than less.

quiz.question: Revenue up 8%, receivables up 40%. What is the most accurate reading?
options: This is a sign that the business is growing very healthily
Receivables outpacing revenue always means accounting fraud
The debt ageing and customer concentration need checking
Nothing to worry about here, since both figures are positive
quiz.explanation: A large gap between the growth rate of receivables and of revenue is a warning sign that calls for further investigation, not yet a final conclusion - but it is not something to wave through either. Fraud is one possible explanation among several, and far more often the cause is looser credit terms or a customer paying more slowly. That both numbers are positive tells you nothing: it is the difference between them that carries the information.

quiz.question: Why is high customer concentration more worrying than a large receivable spread across many small customers?
options: Because concentration risk does not affect the cash flow
Because losing one big customer drives a large bad-debt provision
Because small customers hardly ever pay their invoices late
Because a spread-out receivable is always audited more closely
quiz.explanation: This is the essence of concentration risk: the damage does not spread out but lands in a single event, making the financial impact far greater than with a diversified exposure. Small customers do pay late, but their defaults arrive as a predictable rate rather than one shock, and audit scope is driven by materiality thresholds rather than by how many customers a balance is spread over.

quiz.question: A company books a provision for doubtful receivables. How does this affect the statements?
options: No impact on profit at all, since this is only a balance sheet entry
Cuts both profit and cash by exactly the amount of the provision recorded
Cuts profit in the period but does not reduce cash at that point
Recorded in the notes only, and never in the primary financial statements
quiz.explanation: A provision is a non-cash expense: the money had already failed to arrive, and the accounting is merely acknowledging it. That is why it is added back when computing operating cash flow - and it is also why provisioning late or provisioning short is such a convenient way to smooth reported profit.

keyTakeaways: Receivables are the line to examine when judging quality of earnings
Concentration risk can drive bad debt higher
Revenue is not the same thing as cash received

sections.text: A business showing attractive revenue growth on paper can still carry a serious risk if most of that revenue depends on a handful of customers.
Concentration risk and the quality of earnings

Large receivables concentrated in a few customers can make revenue look attractive while carrying high credit risk - if one large customer runs into financial trouble, the business may have to book a large and unexpected bad-debt provision. Investors normally demand a larger margin of safety, or value the business more conservatively at a lower multiple, where customer concentration risk is high.

items: Receivables growing faster than revenue suggests collection is slowing down
High concentration risk (dependence on a few large customers) is a real business risk, not merely an accounting issue
Receivables are one of the lines to examine most closely when assessing quality of earnings

sections.title: Comparing receivables growth with revenue growth
sections.equation: Warning ratio = % growth in receivables ÷ % growth in revenue

example.title: Worked illustration
example.result: A ratio of 4.5 times - a clear warning sign
example.explanation: Receivables growing nearly five times faster than revenue means the business is selling on credit far more than before, or customers are paying more slowly. Either possibility calls for a careful look at the debt ageing and at customer concentration before you trust the revenue growth figure.

sections.text: Three questions when you find high customer concentration

items: What percentage of revenue comes from the largest customer, and from the top three combined?
Is the ageing of receivables from that customer group stretching out or holding steady?
Has the doubtful-debt provision risen in line with this concentration risk, or is it oddly unchanged?

sections.label: Why the market pays less for customer concentration risk
sections.text: A business with thousands of small customers barely notices losing one. A business where a single customer is 40% of revenue can lose almost half its revenue on one decision by a third party it does not control, should that customer hit financial trouble. This is why investors typically demand a larger margin of safety, or accept a lower multiple, for businesses with high concentration risk.

lines: Attractive revenue does not mean the cash has actually arrived.
Always ask the follow-up: how many customers does that revenue come from, and are they good for it?

practicePrompt.question: When PVGas's trade receivables are heavily concentrated in a few power and fertiliser corporations (concentration risk), what is the biggest financial risk?
options: Late payment risk, or bad debt spreading down the chain
No impact at all, because PVGas is a large company
Revenue will certainly double
Gas prices automatically fall 50%
practicePrompt.explanation: Concentration risk arises when most of the revenue or receivables depend on a few large customers. If one counterparty pays late, the cash flow of the whole business is affected.
